R02.text: Your patterns over the recent 14 days closely matched your 28-day baseline. Sleep averaged about 481 minutes in the baseline and 422 minutes overall in the window, but this average reflects two phases: from March 30 to April 5, sleep started after midnight and lasted 357-368 minutes, then from April 6 onward it returned to your typical ~22:35-22:46 start and 474-485 minute duration. Wake time remained fixed at 07:00 throughout. Steps (~7,980), active minutes (~55), resting heart rate (~56 bpm), and HRV (~45 ms) were stable across both periods. The brief late-sleep phase resolved within the window without changes in other metrics.

R03.text: For the first 6 days of your 14-day window, sleep and daily metrics matched your 28-day baseline (sleep ~480 min, steps ~7,976). From April 6 onward, sleep start shifted ~2 hours later (to ~00:35) while wake time stayed at 07:00, reducing sleep by ~120 min/night. Nighttime coverage dropped accordingly. Steps, activity (~55 min), low movement (~450 min), resting heart rate (~56 bpm), and HRV RMSSD (~45 ms) remained stable throughout.

R06.text: Across the 28-day baseline, sleep averaged 481 min (start ~22:39, end 07:00), steps 7976, activity 56 min, RHR 56 bpm, and RMSSD 45 ms. In the 14-day window, sleep was stable through Apr 5. From Apr 6–12, sleep start shifted approximately one hour later (mean ~00:36), reducing sleep duration to 357–368 min per night. Steps, activity, low movement, RHR, and RMSSD remained unchanged across both periods. The late sleep onset persisted through the end of observation without recovery. Cross-metric correlations were weak.

R07.text: Across 28 baseline days, sleep averaged 481 min (start ~22:40, end fixed 07:00), steps ~7976, activity ~56 min, RHR ~56 bpm, RMSSD ~45 ms. In the 14-day window, sleep start shifted abruptly later from Apr 6 onward (to ~00:30-00:43), reducing recorded sleep to ~357-368 min for 7 consecutive nights before partial return. Steps, activity, low movement, RHR, and RMSSD remained stable. The sleep reduction coincided with reduced nighttime coverage (~377-388 min vs ~500 baseline).

R08.text: For the first six days of your 14-day window, your metrics matched your 28-day baseline: sleep ~480 min starting ~22:40, waking at 07:00, steps ~7,976, active minutes ~56, RHR ~56 bpm, and HRV RMSSD ~45 ms. From April 6 onward, sleep start shifted past midnight (around 00:30–00:43), reducing recorded sleep to ~357–368 min while wake time stayed at 07:00. Steps, activity, RHR, and HRV remained at baseline levels. This pattern suggests truncated nighttime recording rather than a change in daytime metrics.

R09.text: For the first six window days, all metrics matched the 28-day baseline (sleep ~481 min starting ~22:40, steps ~7976, activity ~55 min, RHR ~56 bpm, RMSSD ~45 ms). From day 7 onward, sleep start delayed abruptly to ~00:35 with duration falling to ~364 min, while wake time remained 07:00. Steps, activity, RHR, and RMSSD stayed stable throughout. This late-window sleep shift persisted without recovery.
